Lantern Nights

An eleven-year-old named Mia went on holidays to Taiwan with her family for ten days. Here are some entries from her travel diary.

MONDAY
The wrong order
Dad was sure he remembered the word for 'noodles' from his old textbook, so he marched up to the food stall as though he had ordered there every night of his life. He pointed confidently at the menu and said the word loudly. The woman behind the counter blinked, then laughed so hard she had to hold the counter. Mum, my brother Leo and I watched as she handed Dad a steaming bowl - of pickled cabbage. Dad had asked for 'noodles' but said the word for 'socks' instead. He ate the cabbage anyway, insisting it was 'an adventurous choice.'

WEDNESDAY
Night owls
We were sitting on a bench near the temple, waiting for the lantern parade to begin. It was almost nine o'clock. Suddenly I noticed a group of local children, younger than Leo, wandering past holding their own small lanterns, chattering happily. 'Shouldn't they be in bed?' I whispered. Mum smiled as if she knew something I didn't. 'Everyone stays up for the festival,' she said. 'Schools don't start until midday tomorrow.' My mouth fell open. Back home, nine o'clock was already far too late for anyone under twelve.

FRIDAY
Lantern trouble
At our family friends' apartment, Leo and I were told to leave our shoes at the door. I'd forgotten, and walked straight in. Auntie Wen gasped and pointed frantically at my feet, then at a small red lantern hanging by the entrance, muttering something quickly. I froze, worried I'd broken some serious rule. She grabbed my sleeve and steered me back outside to remove my shoes. It turned out she wasn't cross about luck or tradition at all - she'd simply noticed I was about to step in a puddle of spilled soy sauce. I laughed so hard at my own paranoia that I nearly tripped over the lantern anyway.

Read Nine Men's Morris and answer questions 14 to 20.

Nine Men's Morris

Long before video games existed, people were already inventing simple strategy games using nothing more than a few pebbles and a shape scratched into the dirt. One of the oldest of these is nine men's morris, a game that has been discovered carved into stone seats, temple roofs and even the boards of ancient ships. Historians have found versions of it in Egypt, Greece, Rome, China and Ireland, some more than three thousand years old.

The game gets its lasting popularity from how little it needs. All you require is a simple board of connected lines and points, and eighteen counters - nine for each player, traditionally one dark set and one light set. Nine men's morris is often compared to a more complicated cousin of noughts and crosses. Instead of forming just one line to win instantly, players try to line up three of their own counters in a row along the board's lines, called a 'mill'. Forming a mill lets a player permanently remove one of the opponent's counters from the board.

MOVING AND WINNING
There are two ways to win nine men's morris: by trapping your opponent's counters so that none of them can move anywhere, or by capturing counters until your opponent has only two left, which makes it impossible for them to ever form a mill.

The game unfolds in two stages. During the placing stage, each player takes turns setting their nine counters down on any empty point on the board. Points are only found where lines cross or end (Diagram 1: a player places a counter on an empty point during the placing stage).

Once all eighteen counters are on the board, the moving stage begins. Players slide one counter at a time, one step along a line, into a neighbouring point - but only if that point is empty (Diagram 2: a counter slides one step along a line to an empty neighbouring point during the moving stage).

BREAKING AND REFORMING A MILL
Whenever you complete a mill, you may remove one enemy counter, as long as it is not itself already part of a mill (unless no other counters remain). A mill cannot be used to capture a piece again on your very next turn. To capture again, you must first break your mill by sliding one counter out of line, then slide it back into position on a later turn - as long as your opponent hasn't blocked the spot in between.

Skilled players sometimes build a devastating setup: two overlapping rows that can each be broken and reformed in turn, letting them capture an enemy counter almost every single move. This vicious formation is nicknamed a 'running mill' (Diagram 3: Black breaks one mill and immediately reforms another, capturing a white counter almost every turn. White has little chance to recover).

Nine Men's Morris

Long before video games existed, people were already inventing simple strategy games using nothing more than a few pebbles and a shape scratched into the dirt. One of the oldest of these is nine men's morris, a game that has been discovered carved into stone seats, temple roofs and even the boards of ancient ships. Historians have found versions of it in Egypt, Greece, Rome, China and Ireland, some more than three thousand years old.

The game gets its lasting popularity from how little it needs. All you require is a simple board of connected lines and points, and eighteen counters - nine for each player, traditionally one dark set and one light set. Nine men's morris is often compared to a more complicated cousin of noughts and crosses. Instead of forming just one line to win instantly, players try to line up three of their own counters in a row along the board's lines, called a 'mill'. Forming a mill lets a player permanently remove one of the opponent's counters from the board.

MOVING AND WINNING
There are two ways to win nine men's morris: by trapping your opponent's counters so that none of them can move anywhere, or by capturing counters until your opponent has only two left, which makes it impossible for them to ever form a mill.

The game unfolds in two stages. During the placing stage, each player takes turns setting their nine counters down on any empty point on the board. Points are only found where lines cross or end (Diagram 1: a player places a counter on an empty point during the placing stage).

Once all eighteen counters are on the board, the moving stage begins. Players slide one counter at a time, one step along a line, into a neighbouring point - but only if that point is empty (Diagram 2: a counter slides one step along a line to an empty neighbouring point during the moving stage).

BREAKING AND REFORMING A MILL
Whenever you complete a mill, you may remove one enemy counter, as long as it is not itself already part of a mill (unless no other counters remain). A mill cannot be used to capture a piece again on your very next turn. To capture again, you must first break your mill by sliding one counter out of line, then slide it back into position on a later turn - as long as your opponent hasn't blocked the spot in between.

Skilled players sometimes build a devastating setup: two overlapping rows that can each be broken and reformed in turn, letting them capture an enemy counter almost every single move. This vicious formation is nicknamed a 'running mill' (Diagram 3: Black breaks one mill and immediately reforms another, capturing a white counter almost every turn. White has little chance to recover).

Beyond the Hedge

I climbed through the gap in the tall hedge that Dad had warned me never to use. Everyone said old Mrs Kowalski's orchard was out of bounds, but the smell of ripening apricots was too much to resist. I crept low along the fence line, past a row of sleepy beehives, until I could see the little stone shed at the centre of the orchard. Nobody was around. I tiptoed towards the nearest tree, about to reach for the lowest branch, when a door creaked and a shadow moved across the grass. I dropped flat behind a wheelbarrow. Mrs Kowalski shuffled out holding a chipped enamel bowl, which she set down carefully near the shed. She made a soft clicking sound with her tongue, and within moments a scatter of speckled hens came running from every direction, flapping and squabbling over the scraps. She didn't stay long; she disappeared back inside almost immediately. I stood up and crept past the shed like a burglar tiptoeing away from a crime scene. The hens barely noticed me. Their heads bobbed steadily as they pecked. I walked past the old well and the rusted plough at the side of the shed.

The trickiest part was getting past the geese that patrolled the bottom paddock. The moment I appeared, they began honking furiously and wouldn't stop until I reached the narrow creek at the edge of the property. I rolled up my trousers and waded in. The mud squelched coolly around my ankles. I pushed through a thick stand of reeds, using both hands to keep my balance. The reeds scraped my arms, but the creek water was pleasantly cold after the walk. Only near the deepest point did the water reach my knees. Little clouds of silt rose around my feet with every step.

'This beats sitting inside on a hot afternoon,' I thought, feeling the mud cool between my toes. 'Better than being stuck at home with nothing but a stack of chores.' I imagined my cousins back in the city, stuck in their apartment with the fans going. Dragonflies zipped low across the water, and even though there wasn't a breath of wind, the surface of the creek rippled every so often. The air was thick with the drone of insects and the occasional plop of a frog.

Tech know: Microwave ovens

ACCIDENTAL DISCOVERY
In the 1940s, an American engineer named Percy Spencer was working on radar equipment when he noticed something odd: a chocolate bar in his pocket had completely melted. Curious about what had caused it, he decided to test the invisible waves from the radar equipment on other foods. When he pointed the machine at a handful of popcorn kernels, they began popping almost immediately. Percy's accidental discovery eventually led to the invention of the microwave oven, which today sits in kitchens all over the world.

HOW DOES IT WORK?
Inside every microwave oven is a device called a magnetron, which produces the invisible microwaves used for cooking. The inside walls of the oven are lined with metal, which reflects any microwaves that are not absorbed by the food straight back towards it, rather than letting them escape.

Food contains tiny molecules that behave a little like miniature magnets, with a positive end and a negative end. As microwaves pass through the food, these molecules twist rapidly back and forth to keep lining up with the changing waves. It is this constant twisting and rubbing of molecules against each other that produces heat, cooking the food from the inside as well as the outside.

Water molecules react to microwaves far more strongly than fat or sugar molecules do, which is why moist food heats up more quickly than dry food. This is also why frozen food should usually be thawed slightly, or have a small amount of water added, before microwaving - the water molecules in ice are frozen solidly in place and cannot twist and heat up as easily as liquid water can.

WHAT IS WAVELENGTH?
You may have noticed the small holes in the metal mesh covering a microwave door. Microwaves are far too wide to fit through these tiny holes, but light waves are narrow enough to pass through easily, which is how you're able to watch your food cooking. The distance between the top of one wave and the top of the very next wave is called its wavelength - and it is this measurement that decides whether or not a wave can fit through a small gap.

The Lookout Tower

The year is 3020. The location is a quiet street in a small town called Millbrook.

'Is everyone here?' bellowed Tobias, our self-appointed captain, straightening his recently-inherited cape as he spoke. Six voices mumbled agreement, and someone asked, 'Is this a birthday party?'

'No jokes during a mission briefing,' Tobias tried to boom again, fumbling with the clasp of his cape, which kept threatening to strangle him.

'Today's mission is to build a lookout tower so we can watch for the new kids moving in next door,' Tobias announced.

'We could use some old crates stacked on top of each other,' I suggested.

'That's a terrible idea, Priya,' Tobias declared. Clearly, encouragement was not a skill Tobias had yet developed.

'We'll build it using bricks,' Tobias stated.

'Yes, Tobias. Whatever you say, Tobias,' we all chorused.

All afternoon we hauled bricks, stacking and wedging them until we had a tower that looked as though it had been designed by a toddler with a grudge. Still, it seemed sturdy enough. The last task of the day involved rolling one particularly large brick towards the tower's base, to use as Tobias's own personal podium for future announcements.

The events that followed are recorded in our (extremely secret) mission log, as follows:
1. After a gentle push, the brick gathered speed down a slight slope.
2. The brick rolled onwards (rapidly) towards the tower.
3. The brick struck the tower's foundation, and the foundation shifted.
4. The bricks above tumbled outward like dominoes, flattening Mr Yorke's prize-winning tomato stakes.
5. Without a word to each other, we all fled the scene immediately. Tobias somehow had a head start on the rest of us.

Weeks later, I overheard my mother talking to Mr Yorke about the disaster. 'It must have been that freak gust of wind we had that afternoon,' Mr Yorke insisted loudly. I recognised the voice - it was Tobias's own father. The other parents nodded along sympathetically. Tobias must get his gift for confident leadership from his father, I decided, since neither of them let the facts get in the way of a good story.

Many of the world's most treasured paintings are hundreds of years old, yet they still hang proudly in galleries today. But is there more to an old painting than what we see on the surface? And how do experts make sure these fragile artworks survive for future generations?

Amelia Cho is a paintings conservator at a major city gallery. Her job is to examine old paintings using a range of scientific techniques whenever they arrive for restoration.

'This sometimes uncovers sketches hidden underneath the visible paint, or changes the artist made partway through,' she explains. 'A few years ago, we examined a painting believed to be an ordinary portrait from the 1600s. Using X-ray imaging, we discovered it was actually painted over an earlier, unfinished portrait of a completely different person.'

Amelia's team has also studied the ground layer - the layer beneath the paint - of paintings once thought to be the work of famous artists. 'One painting was long believed to be a self-portrait by a well-known Italian painter,' she says. 'But the ground layer turned out to be a type only ever used in a workshop many kilometres away, so the painting couldn't have been made where everyone assumed.'

DAMAGE CONTROL
Amelia says the most common form of damage to old paintings is accidental. 'Dents, scratches and tears are the things we see most often,' she says. 'There are also gradual changes to the paint's colours, since varnishes and oils used in old paintings can discolour over time. This isn't really damage, but it does change how a painting looks.'

So how do conservators fix paintings and keep them that way? 'We do it in two ways: conservation and restoration,' Amelia explains. 'Conservation covers every way we protect a painting, including how it's handled, transported, stored and displayed.' Old paintings are often made from materials that were once alive, such as canvas made from plant fibres or wooden panels. Since living materials naturally contain water, artworks made from them can be damaged by changes in the surrounding air. 'If a room is too hot or too humid, the paint can crack or peel off.
